Samsung Electro-Mechanics Expands Beyond MLCCs into Silicon Capacitor Business

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is in discussions with multiple global Big Tech companies to supply silicon capacitors (Si-Cap) for AI servers. The company is rapidly emerging as a major supplier alongside Japan's Murata and Taiwan's TSMC.

On the 11th, Samsung Electro-Mechanics held a technology seminar at the Taepyeongno Building in Jung-gu, Seoul, where it shared its silicon capacitor technology and commercialization roadmap. Kim Won-gi, head of Samsung Electro-Mechanics' Si-Cap Development Group, said, "Global Big Tech companies whose names you would immediately recognize are reviewing the adoption of silicon capacitors," adding, "Because the market is formed around a small number of players, Samsung Electro-Mechanics is also aggressively pursuing sales activities."

The silicon capacitor market is led by Japan's Murata and Taiwan's TSMC. Barriers to entry are high because the business requires both semiconductor wafer process and passive component capabilities, and the number of suppliers is limited. Samsung Electro-Mechanics President Chang Duck-hyun is cultivating silicon capacitors as a core growth business in the company's push into the AI market.

The company made its full-scale entry into the market last year as it began supplying customers. It supplied products for the AI accelerators of Marvell—a leader in custom networking chips (ASICs)—and for the package of Samsung Electronics' mobile application processor (AP), the Exynos 2600, among others. More recently, it secured a supply contract worth 1.5 trillion won from a global Big Tech company—the largest single contract in Samsung Electro-Mechanics' history. The related revenue is scheduled to be reflected in earnings starting in 2027.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics presented a "total solution" strategy—bundling its silicon capacitor, multilayer ceramic capacitor (MLCC), and package substrate businesses—as a differentiating factor. Silicon capacitors are mounted inside or adjacent to the package substrate. By supplying both products together, Samsung Electro-Mechanics can design and optimize the package and components simultaneously. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is the only company that operates both passive component and package substrate businesses.

Rather than building large-scale production facilities, the company has chosen a design-centric strategy. It employs a fabless model, outsourcing wafer production to foundries and componentization to specialized semiconductor back-end (OSAT) firms, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics handles product design, testing, and quality verification. The company has a silicon capacitor design and development organization at its Central Research Institute in Suwon.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics' silicon capacitors are manufactured on a 300-millimeter (mm) wafer basis.

A silicon capacitor is a passive component made from a silicon wafer. It temporarily stores electricity and supplies it when needed, keeping the voltage inside the semiconductor package stable. Whereas conventional MLCCs secure capacitance by stacking multiple layers of ceramic, silicon capacitors bore microscopic holes into a wafer and place electrodes inside them. This allows the thickness to be reduced to 100 micrometers (㎛) or less.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics drew its business idea from DRAM technology. DRAM uses a capacitor inside each cell to store data. Samsung Electro-Mechanics developed the silicon capacitor by taking just the capacitor portion of this structure and advancing it into a separate component. The fine-process technology it accumulated while shrinking DRAM circuit linewidths was transferred directly into silicon capacitor development. The more microscopic holes formed in the wafer, the greater the capacitance a silicon capacitor can achieve.

There are differences in silicon capacitor technology between competitors. Samsung Electro-Mechanics utilizes a DRAM-based structure, while TSMC is known to use a logic-process-based trench structure. Samsung Electro-Mechanics mass-produces its products on a 300mm wafer basis, the type primarily used for memory semiconductors.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics projected that the silicon capacitor market will grow at an average annual rate of more than 18%. Its scope of application is expanding from a mobile focus into AI servers, automotive electronics, aerospace, and optical communications. AI servers in particular are emerging as the largest source of demand, as power density increases and package integration intensify simultaneously.

Kim said, "The higher semiconductor performance becomes, the more important power stabilization becomes," adding, "Silicon capacitors will see their range of application continuously expand in the AI server and next-generation high-performance semiconductor markets."

▶ CSP In House ASIC Boom Drives MLCC Specification Concentration; Structural Shortages of High End Specialty MLCCs May Emerge in 2H26, Says TrendForce

- According to TrendForce's latest MLCC industry survey, as the AI competition among global CSPs continues, the adoption of in house ASIC accelerators is accelerating, and as a result, reliance on small form factor, high capacity, high heat resistance MLCCs is expanding.

- Because of this, demand is rapidly concentrating into a limited set of premium specifications, but suppliers' capacity expansion is failing to keep pace with the speed of demand growth, making the possibility of a structural supply shortage in the second half of 2026 an increasingly hard to overlook risk.

- TrendForce emphasizes that next generation AI accelerator platforms are undergoing frequent design changes at the final qualification stage, and that in this process the per board mounting volume of high spec MLCCs is increasing substantially.

- For example, AMD has replaced both aluminum electrolytic capacitors and tantalum capacitors with MLCCs in the BOM of its MI450 platform, and as a result the usage of 47μF 2.5V X6S 0402 MLCCs has increased from 1,440 units per board to 10,544 units.

- Similarly, demand for 100μF 4V X6S 0805 MLCCs on NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform has also increased from 320 units per board to 500 units.

- As the market enters the second half of 2026, mass production of major ASIC platforms such as Google TPU V8t/i, AWS Trainium4, and Meta MTIA 400/450 is expected to ramp up in earnest, and accordingly MLCC demand is projected to reach a new high.

- By contrast, supply growth is failing to keep pace with this demand surge, and signs of supply tightness are already intensifying.

- Murata began mass production of high spec MLCC products such as the 47μF 2.5V X6S 0402 and the 100μF 2.5V X6S 0603 at the end of 2025.

- Samsung Electro Mechanics entered mass production starting in March 2026, and Taiyo Yuden and Kyocera are also expanding output.

- However, these specifications are extremely difficult to manufacture, and significant challenges in securing yield still exist across the industry, creating constraints on any meaningful expansion of actual supply.

- In addition, Murata's new Izumo plant is expected to reach full operation only in 2027, so it is unlikely to provide a meaningful supply easing effect within the current demand cycle.

- The Book to Bill (BB) ratio of major Japanese and Korean suppliers has been rising steadily since April 2026, and lead times for some high capacity X6S products have been extended from the previous 8 weeks to as much as 20 weeks.

- Major CSPs that have already secured long term supply agreements (LTAs) are expected to receive priority allocation.

- By contrast, ODMs and system makers that have not yet secured supply agreements are increasingly likely to face both price premiums on the spot market and shipment delays at the same time.

- TrendForce projects that as multiple demand factors converge simultaneously between the end of the third quarter and the start of the fourth quarter, the possibility of a supply shortage, which until now has remained a potential risk, could turn into an actual market shortage.

- Accordingly, it emphasizes that ODMs need to hurry to secure strategic inventory during the third quarter and to raise their safety stock levels in preparation for potential supply disruptions in the fourth quarter.

Samsung Electro Mechanics Begins Mass Production of FC BGA for Qualcomm's "AI200," Expanding Collaboration into the Data Center Segment

Samsung Electro Mechanics has begun mass production of the package substrate that will be used in Qualcomm's first data center artificial intelligence (AI) accelerator. The supply deal is expected to expand the collaboration between the two companies from its existing footprint in mobile and PC into the data center segment.

According to reporting by ZDNet Korea on the 22nd, Samsung Electro Mechanics recently began mass production at its Busan plant of the flip chip ball grid array (FC BGA) used in Qualcomm's latest AI accelerator, the "AI200."

The AI200 is Qualcomm's first data center AI accelerator, unveiled this past October. It is specialized for AI inference workloads. It is equipped with Qualcomm's in house "Oryon" CPU and "Hexagon" NPU, paired with LPDDR5, a low power DRAM with strong power efficiency.

Qualcomm is targeting the second half of this year for the AI200's launch, and Samsung Electro Mechanics appears to have begun its FC BGA mass production in line with that timeline.

Because the FC BGA that Samsung Electro Mechanics is mass producing for Qualcomm's AI200 is an initial production volume, the volume is reportedly modest for now. Even so, the move is seen as meaningful in that the collaboration between Samsung Electro Mechanics and Qualcomm is expanding from its existing mobile and PC footprint into data center semiconductors. Until now, Samsung Electro Mechanics had supplied the package substrates used in Qualcomm's application processors (AP) for IT devices.

One semiconductor industry official said, "Because Samsung Electro Mechanics has had a long collaboration with Qualcomm, the supply deal for the AI accelerator FC BGA appears to have been concluded smoothly," adding, "Qualcomm plans to release the AI200 this year and the AI250 next year in succession, so Samsung Electro Mechanics can also enjoy the benefit of diversifying its customer base accordingly."

LG Innotek is also understood to be pursuing the supply chain for Qualcomm's AI200 FC BGA. Earlier, at a media event on the 17th, LG Innotek stated that "mass production of FC BGA used in server training and inference semiconductors is targeted for next year."

Another official said, "The AI200, which is specialized for AI inference, requires lower performance specifications for its FC BGA compared with high bandwidth memory (HBM) based AI accelerators," adding, "so the barrier to entry should be comparatively low even for LG Innotek, a latecomer in the FC BGA industry."

FC BGA is a package substrate that connects the semiconductor chip and the substrate via "flip chip bumps" (a method of flipping the chip over). Compared with the wire bonding that was mainly used in conventional packages, it has superior electrical and thermal characteristics, so demand is high, centered on high performance semiconductors.

The AI200 FC BGA is formed with internal layers in the low to mid teens. FC BGA is structured by stacking copper wired circuit layers and an insulator called Ajinomoto Build up Film (ABF) layer upon layer, and the higher the layer count, the higher the performance. For ultra high performance data center AI accelerators, more than 20 layers must be stacked.

▶ AI server demand drives sharp price gains in high end MLCCs

- Rising demand for AI server buildouts is tightening global supply of high end MLCCs, triggering sharp price spikes in China's electronic component distribution market.

- Spot prices for some popular MLCC products have climbed 3 to 5x since the start of the year, and in Shenzhen and Shanghai there is even speculative trading in which some product prices shift on a daily basis.

- The price gains are concentrated in high capacity, high temperature products such as 22μF and 47μF. Unlike the broad based shortage of 2018, the core issue this time is an imbalance between surging AI demand and limited supply.

- Major global players such as Murata and Samsung Electro Mechanics have recently scaled back production for consumer electronics such as smartphones and PCs, shifting capacity toward high margin products for AI servers and automotive applications.

- High end MLCCs carry high technical barriers and demanding yield requirements, making it structurally difficult to add new capacity quickly. Some AI server MLCCs have risen from around 80 yuan per 1,000 units at the start of the year to more than 350 yuan.

- Original manufacturers are managing shipments more tightly than before, with orders of several million to tens of millions of units being filled at only 10 to 20% of the requested volume.

- Some overseas suppliers have revived bundling, requiring buyers of high capacity MLCCs to also purchase mid and low capacity products.

- AI servers use roughly 8 to 12x more MLCCs than standard servers. Goldman Sachs projects that MLCCs are the third largest cost item in AI servers after GPUs and memory, and that related demand will grow 4.3x from 2025 to 2030.

- That said, the price gains are concentrated in high capacity, high reliability products for AI and automotive applications rather than across the entire product range. Demand for low capacity consumer electronics MLCCs remains weak.

- Because building high end production lines takes 18 to 24 months, the shortage is likely to persist through the second half of this year and beyond 2027. China's Fenghua Advanced Technology and Chaozhou Three Circle Group could benefit as orders shift their way.

Samsung Electro Mechanics Sees Its Value Rise as It Pursues 320 Million Dollar AI MLCC Supply Deal With Big Tech

Samsung Electro Mechanics is moving to supply global big tech with several hundred billion won worth of multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCC) for artificial intelligence (AI) servers. As the AI supercycle (a period of exceptional boom) spreads beyond semiconductors into electronic components, Samsung Electro Mechanics is expected to gain momentum in its earnings recovery as well.

According to industry sources on the 28th, Samsung Electro Mechanics is reportedly in final stage discussions ahead of an AI server MLCC supply contract with a US cloud service provider (CSP). The contract is estimated to be worth around 500 billion won (320 million dollars). Major CSPs such as Google, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Meta have recently been competing to build out AI data centers, and the industry believes the counterparty is most likely one of these companies.

MLCC is a core component that stably supplies and controls electric current within the circuits of electronic products. Its range of application is widening beyond information technology (IT) devices such as smartphones and PCs to AI servers and automotive electrical and electronic equipment. In particular, because AI servers carry large numbers of high performance semiconductors such as graphics processing units (GPU), high bandwidth memory (HBM), and central processing units (CPU), power density has risen sharply, driving a surge in demand for high capacity, high reliability MLCC.

Once supply ramps up in earnest under this contract, the pace of Samsung Electro Mechanics' earnings improvement is expected to accelerate further. AI server MLCC is technically more difficult than the mobile variety, but it sells for at least three times more and is used in far greater volumes. A smartphone typically carries 1,000 to 1,300 MLCCs, whereas an AI server computing board uses 15,000 to 25,000 per board. The latest AI servers are equipped with around 20 computing boards, so a single server is said to require hundreds of thousands of MLCCs.

Market growth is also steep. According to market research firm MarketsandMarkets, the global AI server market is projected to grow to 837.8 billion dollars (about 1,150 trillion won) by 2030. Meanwhile, much like memory chips such as DRAM, MLCC supply is failing to keep pace with demand. Jang Duk hyun, president of Samsung Electro Mechanics, said at the regular shareholders meeting this past March that "with rising data center investment, the supply and demand for high capacity, high reliability MLCC is tightening," adding that "we are in discussions with customers to expand supply in line with market conditions."

As a seller's market takes shape, the pricing power of major players including Samsung Electro Mechanics and Japan's Murata, TDK, and Taiyo Yuden has also strengthened. Prices for some MLCC products have already been raised, and long term supply agreements (LTA) are reportedly being signed one after another. In its MLCC business, which accounts for more than 45 percent of total revenue, Samsung Electro Mechanics is focusing on improving profitability by expanding the share of high capacity, high performance products. It is regarded as having secured top tier global competitiveness in AI server MLCC.

Against this market backdrop, analysts forecast that the operating profit of the Component Solutions division, which oversees Samsung Electro Mechanics' MLCC business, will surpass 1 trillion won this year, up more than 70 percent from last year (about 600 billion won). There is also talk of the possibility of reaching operating profit in the low to mid 2 trillion won range next year, roughly double that level. Samsung Electro Mechanics currently conducts MLCC research and development and raw material production at its Suwon and Busan sites, and operates production subsidiaries in Tianjin, China, and the Philippines as mass production bases. A plant expansion is also underway in the Philippines to increase MLCC capacity.

>> TrendForce: Monthly Shipments by Korean and Japanese MLCC Makers Hit Record High on AI Demand; Spillover in Consumer Orders Becomes Visible

• According to TrendForce’s latest MLCC industry survey, strong AI demand drove Murata, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Taiyo Yuden—the three leading Korean and Japanese suppliers—to record their highest monthly shipment volumes in five years in June 2026. Meanwhile, continued spillover in consumer orders pushed up prices at other manufacturers and across distribution channels.

• As Korean and Japanese suppliers rapidly shift consumer-grade X5R capacity toward higher-spec X6S/X7R products for AI applications, capacity for mid- to high-capacitance consumer MLCCs (1µF–22µF) is coming under pressure. Inventory levels for key products have generally fallen to 30 days or less.

• Supply constraints have triggered a surge in urgent orders from distributors, agents, and Tier 2 and Tier 3 customers, further amplifying the order-spillover effect. As a result, order visibility at other manufacturers has improved markedly, accompanied by higher product prices. Distributors that had built inventories in advance have raised prices by an average of 20–25%, while spot-market prices have climbed to two to three times their previous levels. The consumer MLCC market is therefore exhibiting a structural divergence in which end demand remains weak while distribution-channel prices stay firm.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics to Raise MLCC Prices

- Samsung Electro-Mechanics has sent customers a notice announcing that it plans to raise prices for certain MLCC products by 30% from August 1, 2026.

- The company explained that structural growth in global electronics demand has placed pressure on the supply chain beyond what it can absorb internally.

- Samsung Electro-Mechanics said that although it has continued to improve manufacturing efficiency and expand capacity, price adjustments for certain products have become unavoidable to maintain product quality and a stable supply.

- The price increase will apply to all MLCC products under Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ Markup Business Code, with the new prices taking effect for shipments made on or after August 1, 2026.

- The company emphasized that the price adjustment is unavoidable and said it will continue to supply high-quality products and support its customers’ businesses.

- Taiyo Yuden is also moving to raise MLCC prices from September 1, while noting that it may be unable to guarantee customers’ requested delivery schedules.

- Taiyo Yuden explained that it decided to adjust prices because ongoing increases in raw-material costs could no longer be absorbed through cost-cutting efforts alone.

- Even after the price adjustment, supply is expected to remain insufficient to fully meet demand, and the company may still be unable to guarantee on-time delivery.

[Four Key Questions from Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ Conference Call]

Q1) (Company-wide) What is the outlook for Q3 earnings?

A1) In Q2, the company delivered year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter growth, driven by increased sales of high-value-added MLCCs and FC-BGAs for AI servers, networking, and automotive applications, as well as an improved product mix resulting from a higher proportion of premium products.

In Q3, robust demand for related components is expected to continue, supported by sustained investment in AI data centers and advances in autonomous driving. Supply-demand conditions for MLCCs and FC-BGAs are also expected to tighten further.

For MLCCs, the company plans to actively expand the supply of high-value-added, premium-priced products for AI servers, networking, and ADAS applications, including ultra-high-capacitance, high-temperature, and high-voltage products. It will continue discussions on strategic long-term supply agreements with major hyperscalers and semiconductor companies, while also responding proactively on pricing in light of supply-demand conditions.

For FC-BGAs, the company plans to actively expand mass production of new products for AI accelerators and server CPUs supplied to global big tech companies, as well as the supply of high-end products for data centers. It will also continue price negotiations reflecting market conditions. Domestic and overseas capacity expansions tied to LTA discussions with top-tier semiconductor customers will proceed as planned.

For camera modules, the company plans to increase the supply of high-value-added automotive products designed for increasingly advanced ADAS applications and ramp up mass production of new products for humanoid robots.

In Q3, the continued tightening of supply-demand conditions for high-value-added products such as MLCCs and FC-BGAs, the expansion of LTAs, and higher average selling prices are expected to drive record-high earnings.

These trends are expected to continue into Q4 and strengthen further in 2027, supporting sustained earnings improvement.

The company will focus its capabilities on high-growth markets such as AI data centers and automotive applications, while responding quickly to changes in market conditions and supply chains through measures including proactive capacity expansion.

In new business areas such as silicon capacitors and glass substrates, the company will further strengthen collaboration with global big tech customers and proceed with its preparations for commercialization over the medium to long term.

Q2) (MLCC) What is the potential for additional supply agreements for AI-related MLCCs, and what is the company’s future capacity strategy?

A2) The AI server MLCC market is expected to maintain rapid growth as the continued expansion of hyperscaler data-center investment, improvements in GPU computing performance, and faster server-network speeds drive increasing adoption of cutting-edge, high-end MLCCs.

Cutting-edge products, including ultra-high-capacitance products of 100㎌ or more and high-temperature products rated at 125°C, require the highest levels of technology in terms of both performance and reliability. Only a small number of suppliers, including the company, are capable of meeting these requirements. As a result, supply-demand conditions are becoming increasingly tight, while demand for long-term supply agreements to secure stable supply volumes is rising among major AI server customers.

The company has completed LTAs with around 10 customers, including top-tier hyperscalers and major semiconductor companies, and is actively responding to additional LTA requests from key customers.

To strengthen its leadership in the AI server MLCC market, the company is improving yields and productivity while expanding Capex compared with previous years to establish a production base capable of maximizing supply.

As technical requirements for AI server MLCCs advance rapidly, the company will leverage its ultra-high-capacitance product portfolio to launch cutting-edge specifications across different sizes, voltages, temperatures, and operating conditions in a timely manner, enabling it to respond quickly to customers’ diverse requirements.

The company will reinforce its technological leadership in the AI server MLCC market while continuing to deliver revenue growth that outpaces the market.

Q3) (Silicon Capacitors) The company disclosed a KRW 1.5 trillion silicon capacitor supply agreement in May. What is the market outlook, and is there potential for additional orders?

A3) Silicon capacitors offer superior electrical characteristics compared with MLCCs, including low equivalent series inductance, or low ESL, and are also thinner. They are therefore key components placed in the closest proximity to semiconductor chips within AI server semiconductor packages, supporting overall system performance and stability.

Their applications are expanding from mobile devices to AI data centers, and the market is expected to continue growing as the adoption of silicon capacitors in AI data centers increases.

Based on the complementary characteristics of MLCCs and silicon capacitors, the company is currently discussing additional supply agreements with major AI-related semiconductor companies.

Leveraging its position as the only company worldwide capable of providing MLCCs, silicon capacitors, and package substrates on a turnkey basis, the company intends to take the lead in securing the emerging market and drive substantial revenue growth.

Q4) (FC-BGA) The company is reportedly considering capacity expansion. What are the detailed expansion and future capacity-management plans?

A4) As the AI paradigm shifts from training toward inference, global big tech companies are increasingly developing proprietary semiconductor chips optimized for inference, with the number of participating companies also rising.

As AI semiconductors become more powerful, larger chip sizes and increased HBM adoption are accelerating the transition toward ultra-large and highly multilayered package substrates, further consuming suppliers’ available capacity.

Recently, major customers have also increased their requirements for high-end substrates incorporating features such as embedded components and multi-core designs. Only a small number of suppliers with the necessary mass-production capabilities and technological expertise can meet these requirements, further exacerbating the shortage of high-value-added substrates.

The company is discussing strategic LTAs, including investment support, with most top-tier semiconductor customers involved in AI and data-center applications. Its capacity expansion plans will be based on these agreements.

The company will strengthen collaboration with customers on next-generation product development and concentrate its capabilities on securing differentiated technologies. At the same time, it will proceed with capacity expansion as planned to meet customer demand in a timely manner and expand the business over the medium to long term.

‘MLCC Boom’… Big Three, Including Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Raise Prices One After Another

Prices of multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), often called the “rice of IT devices” because of their essential role, are soaring. Demand has surged amid the artificial intelligence infrastructure investment boom, prolonging a supply shortage. The world’s three largest MLCC makers—Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Murata Manufacturing, and Taiyo Yuden—have all recently raised prices and are accelerating capital investment to expand supply. Meanwhile, emerging Chinese manufacturers are moving to take control of the low- to mid-priced commodity market by capitalizing on the MLCC shortage.

MLCC Prices Surge on AI Boom

According to industry sources on the 31st, Japan-headquartered Taiyo Yuden, the world’s third-largest MLCC manufacturer, recently sent customers a letter announcing that it would raise prices for MLCCs shipped from September. This marks its second price increase this year. The company did not disclose the size of the increase.

“We have worked to cut costs in response to rising material and raw-material prices since last year, but the increases have now reached a level we can no longer absorb,” Taiyo Yuden said.

Murata, the global market leader with a 40% share, raised its MLCC prices in March. Samsung Electro-Mechanics, which had been monitoring market conditions, has also decided to raise prices by 30% across its entire MLCC portfolio for shipments beginning on the 1st.

MLCCs serve as “dams” inside electronic devices. They store electricity and then supply it steadily where needed, helping semiconductors operate smoothly. MLCCs are also used in data-center servers, with AI servers requiring particularly large quantities. Because high-performance, high-power semiconductors such as graphics processing units and high-bandwidth memory operate around the clock, more points are needed to distribute electricity reliably.

“Dedicated AI servers use more than ten times as many high-capacitance MLCCs as conventional cloud servers,” an industry official said.

Lead Times for High-Capacitance MLCCs Reach Seven Months

Electronics companies say that securing MLCC supplies has become difficult, even before considering the price increases. According to market research firm Future Electronics, lead times for Murata MLCCs with capacitance of 1 microfarad (μF) or higher had reached as long as 30 weeks as of July. The lead time was 24 weeks in June, meaning it lengthened by six weeks in just one month.

MLCC manufacturers have begun investing in additional facilities to meet demand. During its first-quarter earnings conference call in April, Samsung Electro-Mechanics said, “We expect this year’s investment to more than double from the previous year.” Murata also said in April that it would continue investing to expand its MLCC production capacity.

Industry observers, however, expect the supply shortage to persist for the time being. AI data centers are proliferating rapidly, while only a limited number of companies manufacture MLCCs.

“Even if the three companies, which together account for roughly 70% of the MLCC market, aggressively pursue capital investment, it will be difficult to increase production in the short term,” an industry official said. This is why the MLCC Big Three are expected to continue delivering strong earnings for some time.

There are also forecasts that the MLCC shortage will provide Chinese manufacturers with an opportunity to expand. Sanhuan Group, a leading Chinese company, raised HK$7.16 billion—approximately KRW 1.3 trillion—through its Hong Kong listing in July and plans to build new factories in Thailand and Germany.

China’s Fenghua Advanced Technology has completed a three-phase capital investment program worth CNY 7.5 billion—approximately KRW 1.6 trillion—that began in 2020. The company has expanded its monthly MLCC production capacity to 50 billion units, equivalent to roughly half that of Samsung Electro-Mechanics.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics Flashes Red on Glass Substrate Customer Evaluation... Investment Pushed Back Too

Samsung Electro-Mechanics' investment schedule for semiconductor glass substrates is slipping. A bottleneck has emerged in the customer's prototype reliability evaluation.

As a result, the timeline for building out the production line at GlaSSEM, the glass core joint venture, has also been pushed back, and the timing of related equipment orders has become murky.

According to multiple industry officials on the 12th, GlaSSEM, the glass core joint venture between Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Dongwoo Fine-Chem, has been unable to give its partners an equipment order schedule. One industry official said, "As recently as the end of July the mood was that orders were imminent, but right now it is hard to predict when they will resume," adding, "The schedule has been postponed several times, so at this point it has become difficult even internally to roughly estimate when orders will be placed."

Samsung Electro-Mechanics had been conveying equipment orders to partners for the GlaSSEM production line since November last year, but the schedule was pushed back at least three times, to December last year, then March, then June this year. After June, guidance on any follow up schedule disappeared altogether.

The industry points to the failure to obtain reliability evaluation certification for the glass substrate prototype from a global communications chip customer. A person familiar with the matter said, "I understand that the investment schedule was halted because Samsung Electro-Mechanics failed to pass the reliability evaluation," and "Since the prototype has to be remade and resubmitted, further delays to the existing schedule are unavoidable." The person added, "Because a new prototype cannot be produced within one or two weeks, whether the line investment happens within this year is also uncertain."

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is currently making glass substrate prototypes at its Sejong campus. To move to initial volume production, the step after pilot production, it is preparing to build a production line at GlaSSEM, the joint venture with Dongwoo Fine-Chem, a subsidiary of Japan's Sumitomo Chemical. Selection of the main process equipment suppliers, covering deposition, etching, laser drilling and inspection, is mostly complete.

Last month, expectations ran high among equipment makers that orders would begin in August. Samsung Electro-Mechanics had planned to start with deposition tools, which carry the longest lead times, bring the main process equipment into Dongwoo Fine-Chem's Pyeongtaek campus and install it by April next year, and complete the initial production line within the second quarter. It is also known to have considered placing orders for long lead time equipment under the Samsung Electro-Mechanics name first and then transferring the contracts to GlaSSEM.

A delay to Samsung Electro-Mechanics' glass substrate mass production timeline has likewise become unavoidable. Even if orders are placed within this year, factoring in equipment build times, the production line would be ready in the second half of next year at the earliest. The start of mass production is understood to have been pushed out to 2028 or later.

When GlaSSEM was established early last month, Samsung Electro-Mechanics presented a target of operations starting in the second half of 2027. At the recent second quarter earnings announcement, less than a month later, it revised the start of operations to 2028.
